articles.title: Battle of Chile director Patricio Guzmán dies aged 85
articles.summary:
Passionate documentary maker won international acclaim for unsparing but poetic films exploring the impact of the Pinochet regime in Chile

Patricio Guzmán, the film-maker who chronicled Chile’s bloody 1970s political strife and its subsequent social and political turmoil in films such as The Battle of Chile and Nostalgia for the Light, has died aged 85. According to Chilean news outlet Emol, Guzmán died on Tuesday in Paris after a cardiorespiratory arrest.

Guzmán’s chief preoccupation throughout his career was the carnage unleashed by Augusto Pinochet’s coup in 1973 against Salvador Allende, Chile’s elected president. He later told the Guardian: “I’m a film-maker who was very marked by the ways of the dictator. It has remained with me for ever. I cannot leave it behind.” However, he resisted the idea that he was an activist, political film-maker, adding: “I’m not a sociologist. Neither am I a politician. I make films that are metaphorical and poetic; I interpret reality through my own personal way of looking.”

articles.title: Turkey to halt Iranian Mahan Air flights over US sanctions risk
articles.summary:
Turkey to halt Iranian Mahan Air flights over US sanctions risk

Submitted by Ragip Soylu on Fri, 09/18/2026 - 11:00
Turkish officials say the suspension, which will start on 21 September, is not part of a broader ban on Iranian airlines, but other carriers remain under review
An Airbus A310-304 aircraft belonging to the Iranian airliner Mahan Air sits on the tarmac after landing at Sanaa International Airport in the Yemeni capital on 1 March 2015 (Mohammed Huwais/AFP)
Off

Turkey will suspend flights by the privately owned Iranian carrier Mahan Air after the US Treasury sanctioned Turkish ground-services companies earlier this month for supporting the airline, Turkish officials told Middle East Eye.

The officials said on Friday that the ban will take effect on 21 September and will affect all flights by the carrier to and from Iran.

The Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control had announced a comprehensive sanctions package earlier this month targeting Iranian civilian airlines, ground services providers, cargo companies and aircraft parts suppliers.

The sanctions provided a brief grace period for companies to end their dealings with the targeted Iranian firms. They also threatened punitive action against third-country service providers.

Three Turkish companies, S Sistem, Mes Cargo and Sky Phoenix, were sanctioned for providing services to Mahan Air, including supplying aircraft components, offering general sales services and purchasing aircraft.

One official told MEE that the designation of the three Turkey-based companies over their ties to Mahan Air demonstrated that the risk was directly affecting the airline's service chain in Turkey.

"The risk now extends to every Turkish entity providing services to Mahan Air, from airport operations and ground handling to ticketing and banking. This could disrupt services and trigger further investigations," the official said.

Other Turkish officials told MEE that the decision did not amount to a general ban on Iranian carriers.

However, they said Ankara would continue assessing the risks associated with other airlines, taking into account its bilateral aviation agreement with Tehran, flight safety and possible additional US sanctions that could expose Turkish companies to further penalties.

Mahan Air operated frequent flights to Turkey, including at least three flights a day between Istanbul and Tehran.

The airline confirmed on Friday that it would end its flights to and from Turkey from 21 September. It also said it would suspend services to Oman and Georgia.

articles.title: Saudi-Yemen conflict: The notion of an 'American saviour' is dead
articles.summary:
Saudi-Yemen conflict: The notion of an 'American saviour' is dead

Submitted by Trita Parsi on Thu, 09/17/2026 - 18:11
Regional leaders must urgently adopt a new model in which they take primary responsibility for security in the Middle East
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman attends a trade agreement signature ceremony in Paris, France, on 24 August 2026 (Lou Benoist/AFP)
Off

Once again, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman put his faith in US President Donald Trump to defend Saudi Arabia. Once again, Trump let him down.

Last week, as Houthi forces swept Yemen’s Red Sea coast, Mohammed bin Salman called Trump twice and urged him to launch US strikes. Trump refused, offering intelligence and targeting assistance instead.

Why Mohammed bin Salman expected Trump to say yes is anyone’s guess. He had been here before. 

After the September 2019 attacks on Saudi Arabia’s Abqaiq and Khurais oil facilities - attacks the US attributed to Iran - Trump was pressed to retaliate against Tehran. He declined, explicitly telling reporters that he had never promised to protect Saudi Arabia.

Seven years later, the same assumption persists in Riyadh and throughout the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states: when their security is threatened badly enough, Washington will ultimately come to the rescue. But it won’t. 

This assumption is not merely mistaken. The American security order in the Middle East is dead. Pretending otherwise is becoming a danger to the region’s security.

The Iran war has revealed that it is neither reliable nor effective. US bases in GCC countries have proved to be sources of insecurity rather than security. They were supposed to prevent Iran from starting a war against the GCC. Instead, it was the US itself that started the war - against the objections of several GCC states - and within that war, the bases didn’t deter Iran from attacking. 

Rather, the bases served as magnets for Iranian attacks. Today, former CIA director David Petraeus admits these bases are “no longer viable” due to the massive damage Iran has inflicted on them. The US could not protect the bases from Iranian attacks, and consequently, it cannot protect the GCC states.  

Forging a new order

While the American umbrella did provide security for some years, the order underpinning it - centred on Iran’s exclusion and containment - paved the way for the disastrous war we are currently witnessing. The bloc formation it generated and sustained became a source of instability, rather than a protective shield for Washington’s regional partners.

But with every crisis come opportunities. The collapse of the old order offers a chance to forge a new order in the region - one that is centred on inclusive and collective security, rejects bloc formations, and rests on the shoulders of regional powers themselves, rather than being underwritten by external powers.

That means moving away from a system in which the US seeks to organise half of the region against the other half, and towards one in which regional states develop institutions to manage their rivalries. 

The Iran war can be yet another devastating conflict in the Middle East that leaves only a trail of suffering and destruction - or it can become a turning point

Iran cannot be permanently excluded. Israel must have a pathway into the order if it ends the illegal occupation of Palestine. The GCC states cannot remain permanently dependent on Washington. 

Turkey, Pakistan and Iraq cannot be treated as peripheral, and smaller states cannot be expected to thrive or survive by aligning with the right external patron.

This is the premise of the model developed by the Quincy Institute’s Better Order Project: replacing the region’s failed system of deterrence, alliances and outside intervention with an inclusive regional security architecture. 

All of the region’s major nations - including Iran, Turkey, Iraq and other Arab states - would participate in a permanent institution designed to manage, rather than eliminate, their inevitable rivalries. It would establish mechanisms for crisis communication and deconfliction, conflict prevention and mediation, arms control and confidence-building measures, as well as cooperation on shared challenges such as water, climate and economic development. 

Regional states would assume the primary responsibility for regional security, while the US would remain an important external partner - providing diplomatic, economic and, where collectively agreed, security support - without serving as the region’s permanent military guarantor.

Powerful incentive

Crucially, the architecture would not treat the situation in the Gulf as separate from the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. A new security arrangement in the Gulf that leaves the Israeli-Palestinian conflict unresolved would simply reproduce another source of regional instability. 

The ideal model would therefore stipulate that the door for Israel’s inclusion in the order is always open, but the ticket price is the creation of a Palestinian state, based on 1967 boundaries. 

This could provide the most powerful incentive yet for Israel to abandon its futile and illegal occupation of Palestinian land. Unlike the 2002 Arab Peace Initiative, which offered recognition for recognition, or the Abraham Accords that offer normalisation for normalisation, the Better Order proposal offers Israel integration into the region’s security architecture - provided that Palestinian rights to self-determination and statehood are upheld. 

How a pragmatic axis could reshape the Middle East
Read More »

This would also be a win for the US, whose populace has long favoured bringing troops home from the Middle East, amid widespread resentment of American resources being spent in the region, rather than at home. 

The US could remain deeply engaged - diplomatically, economically and strategically - while dramatically reducing the military burden it has carried for decades. Regional states would assume greater responsibility for their own security, but they would do so collectively, rather than through an arms race or competing blocs.

Given the state of the Middle East, these ideas may come across as naive. But it is out of the ashes of some of humanity’s darkest chapters that visionary pathways to security and stability have risen. 

The European Union was born from the devastation of World War II, transforming a centuries-old Franco-German rivalry into the foundation of a common European project. The Helsinki process emerged at the height of the Cold War, when Europe was divided between nuclear-armed adversaries - yet it created rules and institutions for managing that rivalry.

The Iran war can be yet another devastating conflict in the Middle East that leaves only a trail of suffering and destruction - or it can be transformed into a turning point that sets the region on a more peaceful and stable trajectory. 

None of this will happen by accident. It will happen only if regional leaders see their own countries as the answer for the future, rather than phone calls to an illusory American saviour.

articles.title: Houthi leader denies Yemeni group targeted Mecca with drone
articles.summary:
Houthi leader denies Yemeni group targeted Mecca with drone

Submitted by MEE staff on Fri, 09/18/2026 - 09:16
Abdul-Malik al-Houthi accuses Saudi Arabia of a 'major lie' over claim of attack on holy city
Yemeni supporters of the Houthi movement hold portraits of its leader Abdul-Malik al-Houthi during a protest against restrictions imposed by the Saudi-led coalition, in Sanaa in July 2026 (Mohammed Huwais/AFP)
Off

The leader of Yemen's Houthis has denied the group targeted the city of Mecca in Saudi Arabia.

Abdul-Malik al-Houthi said the claim his group attacked the holy city with a drone was a "major lie" and said they were committed to defending Islamic holy sites.

In a televised address, he said that the real threat to Mecca came from the "Zionist enemy", referring to Israel, and said the latest claim was an attempt to shore up support for "military measures imposed on Yemen".

"The real threat is the Zionist enemy, which seeks to target all Islamic holy sites, including Mecca, Medina, and Al-Aqsa Mosque," Houthi said.

"We are ready to confront it as an Islamic alliance."

Ansar Allah, known as the Houthis, took over stretches of Yemen’s coast near the Bab-el-Mandeb strait over the weekend, followed by attacks on the East-West Pipeline, which carries nearly four percent of the global oil supply through Saudi Arabia.

The Saudi government may need five to six weeks to repair damage from a drone attack on the pipeline, according to Reuters. 

The price of oil had already soared last week as a result of a lightning Houthi offensive that put the group in control of Yemen’s side of the Bab el-Mandeb, a key Red Sea chokepoint for Saudi oil shipments. 

The Houthis have said their current offensive is a response to Saudi attacks, including a drone strike on the capital Sanaa.

"At every stage, it has been the one that began the aggression," Houthi said in his speech.

"We are in a defensive position. We are not the ones who initiate aggression."

articles.title: Heavy clashes reported between Yemeni forces and Houthis in Taiz
articles.summary:
Heavy clashes reported between Yemeni forces and Houthis in Taiz

Heavy clashes between Yemeni government forces and Houthi fighters have been reported in Taiz governorate, particularly in the al-Waziyah district around the al-Dharifah intersection, Al Jazeera reported, quoting government military sources. 

Yemeni government forces have said that some 30 Houthi fighters were killed and another 60 have been wounded. 

Government forces also reported air strikes on Houthi positions around al-Dhikra Junction and the al-Damna and al-Rahida areas.

In Mocha, government forces said raids targeted Houthi movements, reinforcements and roads leading to the area in an effort to disrupt supply lines and prevent further advances towards the coast.

The Yemeni army also said it repelled a Houthi attack on its positions in Kahbub after more than three hours of fighting, claiming the assault was pushed back three times and the attackers were forced to retreat.

articles.title: Houthi ballistic missile reportedly hits King Fahd Port in Saudi Arabia
articles.summary:
Houthi ballistic missile reportedly hits King Fahd Port in Saudi Arabia

Yemen’s Houthi forces launched a "powerful ballistic missile attack" on the King Fahd Industrial Port in Yanbu, Saudi Arabia, overnight, Iranian news agency Tasnim has reported. 

The report said the attack caused significant disruption at the port, with footage circulating that purportedly showed destruction at the site.

Tasnim described the reported attack as a powerful strike but did not provide details of the damage or casualties.

The report comes amid heightened regional tensions and a series of Houthi attacks on Saudi targets.

articles.title: Morning update
articles.summary:
Morning update

Good morning Middle East Eye readers,

Here are the latest developments: 

  • South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said that he would not deploy any military assets to the Middle East that could potentially draw Seoul into conflict amid the war on Iran. However, Lee indicated that the government is considering whether to expand its role safeguarding navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, as global energy supplies face severe disruption. 

  • Yemen's army said that 30 Houthi fighters were killed and over 60 others were wounded within 24 hours in the Al-Waziyah district west of Taiz. Yemeni warplanes also reportedly struck Houthi vehicles and gathering points in the area, a military source was cited as saying by the Armed Forces Media Center.

  • Al Jazeera reported that Israeli artillery shelling targeting the town of Haddatha in the Bint Jbeil district in southern Lebanon resulted in a fire breaking out. Israeli attacks across southern Lebanon have continued despite a ceasefire in place.

  • The US State Department has notified Congress that it plans to sell Saudi Arabia up to 48 F-35 warplanes, in a move that has been widely opposed by Israel. The historic sale could total $24.3bn and would mark the first time an Arab state gains access to the US’s fifth-generation jet fighter.

  • The Israeli army warned Benjamin Netanyahu’s government that security lines on three fronts cannot be maintained without "without billions of shekels added to the budget", the Israeli Army Radio reported. The three fronts were identified as the Gaza Strip, the occupied West Bank and Lebanon.

articles.title: Pakistan says time has come to implement Mecca defence pact
articles.summary:
Pakistan says time has come to implement Mecca defence pact

Pakistan’s defence minister has said the time has come to implement the Mecca defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkey as Houthi attacks on the kingdom intensify.

Speaking to Geo News on Wednesday, Khawaja Asif said Pakistan remained committed to defending Saudi Arabia and the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, adding that Islamabad had a duty to protect them even without the agreement.

“Makkah Agreement applies to us, and we will fulfil our duty,” said Asif without elaborating on what Pakistan may do.

Houthi officials have denied targeting the holy city.
